memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.'" — Gen 50:20 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This may be the most important verse in Genesis, and every word of it matters.

"You intended to harm me." Joseph does not soften what they did. It was evil, they meant it, and he names it plainly. Any forgiveness that requires pretending the wrong was not really wrong is not forgiveness at all.

"But God intended it for good." At the same time, and without cancelling the first statement, God had His own intention running underneath theirs. Not merely rescuing something from the wreckage afterwards — intending, purposefully, from the beginning.

Both are true. Human beings are fully responsible for their sin. God is fully sovereign over the outcome. Scripture holds these together without explaining how, and we should not force a resolution the Bible does not give.

"The saving of many lives." That was the purpose. A famine survived, a family preserved, a nation kept alive.

And this exact pattern reaches its fulfilment at the cross. Wicked men crucified Jesus and were genuinely guilty of it — and Peter preached that it happened by God's deliberate plan (Acts 2:23). The worst act in human history became the saving of many lives.

Your suffering is not good. But it is not outside His reach, and it is not wasted.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Is there a wrong done to you that you need to name honestly rather than excuse?
2. Where have you seen God bring good out of something evil?
3. What does the cross teach you about how God works through suffering?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, You do not excuse evil and You are not defeated by it. Help me name wrongs honestly, forgive fully, and trust that You are working good I cannot yet see. Amen.
